article_title: The Effect of TMPT Program on Pre-School Children's Social Problem Solving Skills
citation: Gur, C. & Kocak, N. (2018). The Effect of TMPT Program on Pre-school Children's Social Problem Solving Skills. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 73, 77-94. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2018.73.5
title: Thinking from Multidimensional Perspectives Training Program (TMPT)
description: The TMPT Program is a Thinking Training curriculum the researchers developed for five- and six-year-old children, aiming to "assist children explore by means of stimuli that are interesting to them" such as stories, poems, and arts. It proceeds through five dimensions: self-recognition, recognizing the other, recognition of a third person, group perspective, and social and universal perspective. Each month one dimension is discussed in the classroom and each dimension consists of 20 activities, for 100 activities in total across science, math, music, and story time, each averaging thirty minutes.
requirements: Teachers receive monthly training on how to use the TMPT Program and apply the content in their own classes
The discussion process is central; the adult should not judge the child's ideas and may clarify topics with open-ended questions
constraints: The program was evaluated only with 5-6-year-old preschoolers in Ankara over a five-month period
examples: In the self-recognition dimension, children listen to 'The Little Red Hen' and answer 'If I were the hero of the story, what would I do?'; in the universal perspective dimension, children design a device for a better world.
key_sources: Gur, C. & Kocak, N. (2018). The Effect of TMPT Program on Pre-school Children's Social Problem Solving Skills. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 73, 77-94. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2018.73.5

article_title: Predictive validity of admission tests and educational attainment on preclinical academic performance - a multisite study.
citation: Jaehn M, Hissbach J, Frickhoeffer M, Weppert D, Zimmerhofer A, Hampe W, Kadmon M, Becker N. (2025). Predictive validity of admission tests and educational attainment on preclinical academic performance – a multisite study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07974-2
title: TMS and HAM-Nat admission tests for German medical school selection
description: Two subject-specific cognitive admission tests used by German medical faculties. The TMS comprises eight subtests measuring cognitive abilities relevant to medicine, with internal consistency (Cronbach's Alpha "ranging between 0.91 − 0.92"), and scores standardized to a mean of 100 and SD of 10. The HAM-Nat consists of a natural-science knowledge test weighted 75% plus verbal and numerical reasoning subtests, based on item response theory with theta scores. Both are on-site, proctored, paper-pencil multiple-choice tests; approximately 55% of HAM-Nat knowledge items have been previously published, prompting targeted preparation.
requirements: Administered as proctored on-site paper-pencil tests with items assembled from item banks
constraints: The HAM-Nat was used for selection by only two of the 38 German medical schools during the study period
target_learners: undergraduate medical school applicants in Germany
target_learning_goals: assessing applicant aptitude for medical studies
examples: Since 2020 all German medical faculties admitting through undergraduate entry must use at least one additional selection measure besides high-school GPA, and admission tests are the measure of choice
key_sources: Jaehn M, Hissbach J, Frickhoeffer M, Weppert D, Zimmerhofer A, Hampe W, Kadmon M, Becker N. (2025). Predictive validity of admission tests and educational attainment on preclinical academic performance – a multisite study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07974-2

article_title: Temporomandibular disorder clinical practice teaching through case-based learning with the symptom "limited mouth opening": a pilot study.
citation: Jiang Pan, Chen Haixiang, Li Jing, Zhou Hangtian. (2025). Temporomandibular disorder clinical practice teaching through case-based learning with the symptom “limited mouth opening”: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07429-8
title: Theory-practice gap account of TMD clinical education failure modes
description: The article offers an explanatory account of why residents with adequate theoretical TMD knowledge still underperform clinically, attributing the gap to “three predominant limitations: (1) Compartmentalized Knowledge-Failure to synthesize interdisciplinary concepts and recognize disease interrelationships; (2) Anatomico-Clinical Disconnect-Inability to correlate TMJ structural/functional characteristics with symptomatic presentations; (3) Diagnostic Fragmentation-Deficient capacity for holistic case analysis.” The symptom-focused CBL model is presented as the remedy that integrates knowledge across these failure modes. The account draws on surveys showing dental students and clinicians lack systematic TMD competency, including that 62% of surveyed orthodontists “received inadequate TMD training during residency.”
requirements: Cases that force integration across anatomy, biomechanics, imaging, and psychosocial axes
constraints: Presented as the authors’ interpretation of clinical observations and cited surveys, not as a directly tested mechanism
target_learning_goals: holistic case analysis and systematic TMD diagnosis
key_sources: Jiang Pan, Chen Haixiang, Li Jing, Zhou Hangtian. (2025). Temporomandibular disorder clinical practice teaching through case-based learning with the symptom “limited mouth opening”: a pilot study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07429-8

article_title: Training in the practice of noninvasive brain stimulation: Recommendations from an IFCN committee.
citation: Fried P.J., Santarnecchi E., Antal A., et al. (2021). Training in the practice of noninvasive brain stimulation: Recommendations from an IFCN committee. Clinical Neurophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clinph.2020.11.018
title: TMS core competency set: device operation, coil handling, hotspot identification, and motor threshold assessment
description: The guidelines enumerate core TMS competencies common to most TMS protocols: basic device operation and parameter setting; proper coil handling including placement, returning to a chosen site, and maintaining position and orientation over prolonged stimulation; identification of the motor (and/or non-motor) hotspot; and assessment of resting and active motor threshold using EMG and/or visible twitch, all according to IFCN guidelines. Once mastered, these core skills adapt to other TMS protocols such as paired-pulse or patterned TMS mainly by selecting different stimulation parameters.
requirements: Competencies must be performed according to IFCN guidelines and procedures (Rossini et al. 1994, 2015; Rossi et al. 2009)
constraints: With a few exceptions, such as stimulation of visual areas to elicit phosphenes, these core skills are common to most TMS protocols; special coils for deeper structures necessitate additional training
target_learners: Technicians and trainees beginning TMS practice
target_learning_goals: foundational practical TMS skills applicable across protocols
key_sources: Fried P.J., Santarnecchi E., Antal A., et al. (2021). Training in the practice of noninvasive brain stimulation: Recommendations from an IFCN committee. Clinical Neurophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clinph.2020.11.018
